rv.q: As directed by Lindsay Posner, it struck me as a sharp and loveable play, expertly acted and with enough laughs and relatable family rows to keep afloat its serious moral baggage.
This absorbing revival of Ryan Craig's play from 2011 is also an unravelling, one in which morality and geopolitics play out.
Revivals don't come much better timed than the Menier's fresh staging of Ryan Craig's The Holy Rosenbergs.
This is still a drama that heads in unexpected directions.
This is a play that struggles to contain the weight of the issues — but perhaps that is impossible.
Strong performances hold together this knotty, overstuffed drama about tensions within the Anglo-Jewish community
Despite moments of sardonic mirth, we are left exhausted by circular arguments and claims of righteousness and victimhood.
The trouble is that for all its bracing relevance, the Israel/Gaza stuff is so bombastic as to overwhelm the more nuanced family tragedy.
This is a serious, and at times seriously funny, bid to show how events in Gaza impact Jews elsewhere, but also a clumsy one.
It is gripping, urgent, and deeply humane, and it deserves the attention of anyone who cares about new writing in London.

Read our review of Ryan Craig's play The Holy Rosenbergs, now in performances at the Menier Chocolate Factory to 2 May. “Do the right thing,” a doctor and synagogue grandee says by way of an exit line well into the second act of The Holy Rosenbergs.

Timing is everything. In 2011, Ryan Craig wrote this play about a north London Jewish family being pulled apart by politics against the background of the first Gaza war, the three weeks at the turn of 2009 in which Hamas and the Israel Defence Forces battled in a conflict that left between 1,166 and 1,417 Palestinians and 13 Israelis dead.
This is a strong revival of a play whose resonance has only deepened.
Yet in trying to say everything at once, this revival ends up diluting its strongest ideas.
Great line. Pity about the rest of it.
The Rosenbergs are trapped, like all of us but more paintfully, in this miserable, inextricable angry rift within the human family.
Oberman delivers a masterclass performance, always astonishing to watch, and ensuring the heavy and topical themes land with the impact they deserve.
In that context the play stands out for bringing nuance and complexity to a subject which is debated with verbal baseball bats.

cn.t: Craig's timely family drama about a Jewish household torn apart by the Gaza conflict draws praise for strong performances, particularly Oberman and Woodeson, but divides critics who find it either powerfully relevant or overly contrived and schematic.
